title: Overview
text:
Welcome to Zurafa

Zurafa is a terminal workspace for macOS. The SwiftUI app renders terminals and workspace controls; a Rust daemon owns processes, session layouts, events, and authoritative snapshots. The current public build is 0.1.18 for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 14 or later.

 Find your way around

- [Install on macOS](/docs/install/) covers the download, first launch, and security prompt.
- [Quick start](/docs/quickstart/) walks through a local session, a tab, a split, and the command picker.
- [Sessions, tabs & panes](/docs/sessions/) explains the workspace model and what persists.
- [Files & images](/docs/previews/) covers file previews, image paste, and program icons.
- [Remote SSH](/docs/ssh/) shows how saved hosts and system SSH work.
- [Direct over Tailscale](/docs/remote-access/) connects tabs to tailnet hosts without SSH.
- [Appearance, config & Ghostty](/docs/appearance/) and [Dithered backgrounds](/docs/backgrounds/) cover visual settings.
- [Program status](/docs/status/) explains structured OSC 7501 reports.
- [Architecture & events](/docs/architecture/), the [IPC protocol](/docs/ipc-reference/), and the [CLI](/docs/cli/) document automation surfaces.

 What the beta includes

Multiple sessions, tabs, split panes, focus and zoom controls, file previews, image paste, program icons for coding agents, a plain-text config file, system SSH remote sessions, light and dark appearance, Ghostty themes and color and font import, a Nerd Font symbol fallback, optional dithered image backgrounds, structured terminal status indicators, and an early Rust CLI for daemon automation. The terminal process and workspace state live in the Rust daemon.

 Current limits

This is an Apple Silicon build only. It is signed with Developer ID and notarized by Apple. Open sessions live in daemon memory and do not survive a daemon restart. Zurafa does not yet include Lua scripting, mosh transport, or a native Tailscale integration. [Read the full limits and troubleshooting guide](/docs/troubleshooting/).

title: Install on macOS
text:
Install Zurafa on macOS

The current release supports Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 14 or newer. An Intel build is not available yet.

 Download and install

1. Download [Zurafa 0.1.18 for macOS](/releases/Zurafa-0.1.18-macos-arm64.dmg).
2. Open the DMG.
3. Drag Zurafa.app into your Applications folder and open it.

Zurafa is signed with Developer ID and notarized by Apple.

 Verify the download

To check the DMG in Terminal, run:

sh
shasum -a 256 Zurafa-0.1.18-macos-arm64.dmg


The expected SHA-256 is b4d8126a51205e1c4a0c307808698a6365b2b1114356295f11e0312ce2feccfb.

 What starts with the app

Zurafa connects to a per-user Rust daemon over a Unix socket. If no daemon is running, the app starts the bundled one. Closing the app does not immediately stop that daemon or its terminal processes. Sessions and PTYs remain available while that daemon is alive; they are not restored after it exits.

 Updating from an older build

Zurafa includes Sparkle auto-updates. Use Zurafa → Check for Updates… to update from inside the app. If an older daemon is still running with an incompatible protocol, stop that daemon before launching the new build. Stopping it ends its active terminal processes. See [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/) for the command and its consequences.

title: Quick start
text:
Quick start

This guide gets you from the first launch to a useful local workspace.

 Open a tab

Zurafa begins with a local session called Workspace and creates a terminal tab. It starts your account's configured default shell. Press ⌘T or use the plus button to add another tab.

 Split a pane

Press ⌘D to split the focused pane to the right, or ⇧⌘D to split it downward. Each pane has its own PTY and shell. Click a pane to focus it. Use ⌘[ and ⌘] to move focus, ⇧⌘↩ to zoom or unzoom, and ⌘W to close the focused pane.

 Use the command picker

Press ⌘K to open the command picker. Search for commands such as Change Session, Rename Tab, Add Remote Host, Import Ghostty Settings, or Set Background Image. Press Return to run the selected command, or Escape to close the picker.

 Create another session

Choose New Session from the command picker or press ⇧⌘N. Click the workspace name at the top of the window to open the session picker and switch between sessions.

 Connect to another machine

Choose Add Remote Host from ⌘K, enter a host or SSH address, and create a remote session. Zurafa uses the system SSH client, so your SSH configuration and keys remain in use. See [Remote SSH](/docs/ssh/).

title: Sessions, tabs & panes
text:
Sessions, tabs & panes

Zurafa uses a hierarchy that lets you separate work without losing spatial context. In the backend, a session contains windows and terminal blocks. The macOS app presents these as a workspace session, tabs, and panes.

 Sessions

A session is an independent workspace with a label, tabs, and optional remote host. Use the session picker from the top bar or Change Session in ⌘K. Choose New Session or press ⇧⌘N to create one, Rename Session or press ⇧⌘E to update its label, and Delete Workspace or press ⌥⇧⌘W to end it. Closing a session closes its terminals.

Open sessions live in daemon memory. They remain while the daemon is running, including when the Swift app disconnects, but they disappear on daemon restart. Saved SSH host definitions are stored separately and survive daemon restarts.

 Tabs

A tab is a top-level terminal layout. Add one with ⌘T, the plus button, or the command picker. Select tabs in the top bar or with ⌘1 through ⌘9. Press ⌥⌘T to switch between horizontal and vertical tab bars. Rename the current tab from ⌘K. The Close Tab command is ⌥⌘W and closes every pane in that tab.

 Panes

Split the focused pane right with ⌘D or down with ⇧⌘D. The new pane receives its own shell or SSH process. Resize a split by dragging the divider. Click a pane to focus it; ⌘[ and ⌘] cycle focus. ⇧⌘↩ zooms the focused pane without closing the others. ⌘W closes only the focused pane. Closing one side of a split collapses the layout while the surviving pane keeps its process.

 How layout updates reach the app

The Rust daemon validates and commits each layout command, increments that session's layout revision, and emits a session_view_changed event. The app then reads a fresh authoritative snapshot. Structural events can accompany the revision signal, but the frontend does not reconstruct a full layout by guessing from individual events. [Read the architecture guide](/docs/architecture/).

title: Commands & shortcuts
text:
Commands & shortcuts

The command picker is the quickest way to discover an action. Press ⌘K, type part of a command name, and press Return. The picker also exposes appearance, Ghostty import, background image, and remote-host actions.

 Keyboard shortcuts

 Action  Shortcut 
 ---  --- 
 Command picker  ⌘K 
 New tab  ⌘T 
 Close focused pane  ⌘W 
 Close tab  ⌥⌘W 
 New session  ⇧⌘N 
 Rename workspace  ⇧⌘E 
 Delete workspace  ⌥⇧⌘W 
 Go to directory  ⇧⌘G 
 Refresh sessions  ⌘R 
 Toggle tab layout  ⌥⌘T 
 Open config file  ⌘, 
 Split pane right  ⌘D 
 Split pane down  ⇧⌘D 
 Zoom or unzoom pane  ⇧⌘↩ 
 Next pane  ⌘] 
 Previous pane  ⌘[ 
 Next workspace  ⇧⌘] 
 Previous workspace  ⇧⌘[ 
 Select tab 1–9 (workspace 1–9 while the workspace picker is open)  ⌘1–⌘9 
 Switch light / dark  ⇧⌘A 

 Command picker actions

You can change or rename a workspace, rename a tab, add a remote host, create workspaces and tabs, open a directory in a new local tab, close a tab or workspace, refresh workspaces, switch the tab layout, choose Follow System / Light / Dark, import or clear Ghostty settings, set and toggle a dithered background image, split panes, and toggle pane zoom.

 Input focus

Keyboard input goes to the focused terminal pane when no picker or editor is open. Click inside a pane to focus it. The Rust daemon receives terminal input and owns the PTY process; the Swift app does not launch a second process for a pane.

title: Files & images
text:
Files & images

Zurafa keeps the files your programs mention one click away, and lets you hand images to terminal programs such as coding agents.

 Preview a file

Hold ⌘ and click a file path in terminal output. Relative paths resolve against the pane's current directory. Zurafa opens a preview beside your panes:

- Images show at their full aspect ratio.
- Markdown renders with headings, lists, tables, and syntax-highlighted code blocks.
- Org files (.org) render the same way: headings, lists, tables, links, emphasis, and +BEGIN_SRC blocks. Property drawers, comments, and + keywords other than +TITLE are hidden.
- Math in Markdown and Org renders as typeset LaTeX: $…$ and \(…\) inline, $$…$$, \[…\], and equation/align/gather environments as blocks. Custom macros (\newcommand) are not supported.
- HTML pages render live and can be interactive; see [Interactive pages](/docs/previews/interactive-pages).
- Code and plain text are syntax highlighted in a monospaced view you can select and copy; long lines scroll horizontally.

When the file is inside a git repository, the preview header shows its status (Modified, Untracked, Added, …) and how many lines were added and removed compared with the last commit.

 Interactive pages

HTML files (.html, .htm) render as live pages, so a coding agent can show an explanation you can interact with: an animation you step through, a chart that updates, or Mermaid diagrams drawn in the page.

Elements can hand you a follow-up question. When a page calls window.webkit.messageHandlers.zurafa.postMessage(text), for example from a click on a diagram node, Zurafa pastes text into the prompt of the pane that opened the preview. It is not submitted: edit it or press Enter yourself. Line breaks and control characters are stripped, and the text is capped at 500 characters.

Pages are sandboxed for this: requests to the network are blocked, links do not navigate away, and the page can only read files in its own folder. Put scripts and images it needs beside it. Pages that load scripts or fonts from the web will render without them.

Other programs can open the preview too: zurafa preview PATH shows the file beside the current pane, or beside the focused pane of the active tab when run outside Zurafa. Pass -s and -b to choose another session or pane.

Other file types show a short "no preview available" note. Directories, and paths that do not exist, open with the system default handler instead. Each workspace keeps its own preview, so switching workspaces leaves it behind. Close the preview with its close button.

 Paste an image

Paste (⌘V) while an image is on the clipboard, such as a screenshot or an image file copied in Finder. Zurafa saves it as a PNG in the system temporary folder and types the file path into the focused pane, followed by a space. Programs that accept image paths, such as Claude Code, can then read it.

Pasting text works as usual.

 Program icons

Tabs show an icon for each program running in their panes. Zurafa recognizes Claude Code, Codex, and Pi, including Pi launched through Node or the pi-coding-agent package; everything else shows a terminal icon.

title: Remote SSH
text:
Remote hosts & SSH

Remote sessions connect with the system SSH client, so they use your usual ~/.ssh/config, keys, agent, and known hosts. Shells run in a small Zurafa daemon on the remote machine, so they keep running when the connection drops or your Mac sleeps.

 Add a host

Open ⌘K and choose Add Remote Host. The address field accepts a hostname or SSH alias, user@host:port, or ssh://user@host:port.

If Tailscale is running on this Mac, the sheet also lists your online Linux and Mac tailnet machines. Use ↑↓ and Return, or click one, to save it and connect. Zurafa uses the machine's MagicDNS name when this Mac can resolve it, and its Tailscale IP otherwise (for example when Use Tailscale DNS is off). Tailnet machines are saved without an SSH user, so SSH uses your Mac username unless ~/.ssh/config says otherwise; set the user with the gear icon if it differs.

A saved host appears in the session picker. Selecting it opens or switches to its remote session.

 Sessions that survive disconnects

The first time you open a remote tab, Zurafa installs its daemon on that host over the same SSH connection, under ~/.zurafa/. Builds are included for Linux (x86_64 and arm64) and Apple silicon Macs. Each tab's shell then runs in that daemon:

- When the connection drops, the tab shows Connection lost; reconnecting…, reconnects on its own, and replays what you missed (up to 256 KB per terminal).
- Closing the tab ends the remote shell. When the remote shell exits, the tab shows its exit code.
- The remote daemon stops by itself a minute after its last shell ends.

This needs SSH login without prompts: a key, your SSH agent, or [Tailscale SSH](https://tailscale.com/kb/1193/tailscale-ssh) (sudo tailscale set --ssh on the remote machine). If the host asks for a password, has an unknown host key, can't run the daemon, or prints text when a non-interactive shell starts, the tab says so and falls back to plain SSH. That still works, password prompts included, but the session does not survive a dropped connection.

 Skip SSH on your tailnet

For a Linux host in your tailnet, the bolt button next to a saved host turns on a direct connection: tabs then connect straight to the host's Zurafa daemon over Tailscale and use SSH only as a fallback. [Direct over Tailscale](/docs/remote-access/) explains how it works, HTTPS through Tailscale Serve, and the login server for several accounts.

 Work in a remote session

Create tabs and split panes as you would locally. The session label and host are visible in the top bar and picker. You can keep local and remote sessions open in the same app and switch between them. Remote tabs show program status from OSC 7501 but not the foreground-process icon.

 Saved hosts and session lifetime

Host definitions are stored in ~/Library/Application Support/Zurafa/hosts.json with owner-only permissions. A remote session keeps a copy of its host definition, so removing a saved host does not alter a session already open. Saved host definitions survive daemon restarts. Restarting the Zurafa daemon on your Mac closes its remote tabs, and their remote shells with them.

 Troubleshooting connections

Zurafa validates addresses before saving them and passes SSH arguments separately. Host authenticity and authentication are handled by system SSH.

If a connection fails, first run the same SSH target from macOS Terminal. Check DNS, network reachability, ~/.ssh/config, your keys, and host verification there. To check that the remote daemon can be used, ssh -o BatchMode=yes <host true must succeed without asking for anything. [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/) covers more checks.

title: Direct over Tailscale
text:
Direct over Tailscale

Remote tabs can skip SSH and connect straight to the Zurafa daemon on a host in your tailnet, much like [Rex](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/linux/remote-access). Tailscale encrypts the connection and tells the daemon who is calling, so there are no SSH keys or password prompts, and SSH stays as the fallback.

 How a tab connects

When you open a remote tab, Zurafa checks whether the host resolves to a Tailscale address that your Tailscale knows as a peer. Only then does it try a direct connection, because the direct routes are plain HTTP that is only safe inside WireGuard. It tries each route in turn and uses the first one that answers:

diagram:routes
The first route that answers wins. A tab keeps its route when it reconnects, because its shell lives in that one daemon.


1. HTTPS on port 443 through Tailscale Serve, for .ts.net names. The certificate is checked like any website's.
2. HTTP on port 7297 to the daemon's tailnet listener.
3. The SSH bridge from [Remote SSH](/docs/ssh/): installs the daemon over SSH and survives dropped connections.
4. Plain ssh -tt when the bridge can't run, for example when the host asks for a password.

Direct tabs reconnect like bridged ones: the tab says Connection lost; reconnecting… and replays what you missed. Zurafa pings every 15 seconds and treats 45 seconds of silence as a dropped link.

 Turn on a direct connection

For a Linux host with systemd that you reach over SSH with a key, the app sets everything up:

1. Open ⌘K, find the host under Saved Hosts and click its bolt button.
2. Choose Turn On. The status bar shows Setting up direct connection… and then the result.
3. Open a new tab to that host. It now connects directly.

Over SSH, this copies the daemon to ~/.zurafa/service/, installs a systemd user service zurafa.service, starts it, and runs loginctl enable-linger so it keeps running after you log out. The service listens on the host's Tailscale addresses, port 7297, and on a socket for Tailscale Serve. It admits only your own Tailscale account.

diagram:direct
A direct connection to your own account: HTTP on the tailnet port, or HTTPS through Tailscale Serve. Either way the service checks with Tailscale that the caller is you.


Turn Off stops the service and removes it. Turning it on again after a Zurafa update restarts the service, which ends tabs that use it.

 HTTPS through Tailscale Serve

To also reach the service over HTTPS on the host's .ts.net name, point Serve at its socket once, on the host:


sudo tailscale serve --bg --https=443 unix:/home/<you/.zurafa/service/serve.sock


Other Serve entries on other ports stay as they are. If HTTPS certificates are not enabled for your tailnet yet, Serve prints a link to turn them on. Serve names the caller in a Tailscale-User-Login header and replaces any such header a caller sends itself. It does not name tagged devices, so they can only use port 7297.

 Where Tailscale runs in userspace networking (common in containers), the daemon cannot listen on the Tailscale address itself. It skips it with a warning, and Serve is the way in.

 Who may connect

 Caller  Port 7297  HTTPS via Serve 
 ---  ---  --- 
 You, from any of your devices  Yes  Yes 
 Another person on your tailnet  Only with --tailnet-allow-identified  Only with --tailnet-allow-identified 
 A tagged device  Only with --tailnet-allow-identified  Never 
 The host itself  Yes  Yes 

On a tagged host, which has no owner, only the host itself gets in unless you pass --tailnet-allow-identified. Anyone admitted can run programs as the daemon's user, just as with SSH. Refused callers get HTTP 403, and their tab falls back to SSH.

 Several accounts: the login server

To let people on your tailnet use different accounts on one host, run the login server instead of the per-user service. It runs as root, finds out who each caller is from Tailscale, and starts a session for one local account. There are no passwords: the Tailscale identity is the authentication.

diagram:login
The login server picks an account, then runs runuser -l for it. That opens a PAM session and starts the account's own daemon, which keeps its shells when the login server restarts or is upgraded.


On the host, turn off your per-user direct connection first (both use port 7297), then install it with sudo:


sudo "$HOME/.zurafa/$(ls -t ~/.zurafa  head -1)/zurafa-daemon" install-login-server
sudo tailscale serve --bg --https=443 unix:/run/zurafa/serve.sock


This installs zurafa-login-server.service and, if it doesn't exist yet, /etc/zurafa/accounts.jsonc, which gives the account you ran sudo from to the machine's Tailscale owner. Edit the file to decide who may use which account. It allows comments and trailing commas, and changes apply to the next connection:


{
  "version": 1,
  "accounts": {
    "alice": { "principals": ["tailscale:alice@example.com"] },
    "root": { "principals": ["tailscale:alice@example.com"] },
    "guest": { "principals": ["tailscale:tag:ci", "anonymous"] },
  },
  "defaults": { "tailscale:alice@example.com": "alice" },
}


 Principal  Matches 
 ---  --- 
 tailscale:<login  One person, by Tailscale login 
 tailscale:tag:<tag  Devices with that Tailscale tag 
 tailscale:  Any person on the tailnet (never a tagged device) 
 tailscale:tag:  Any tagged device 
 identified  Any caller Tailscale can name 
 anonymous  Callers on a plain listener started with --allow-anonymous 

The account "" grants every regular account (user ID 1000 or higher) to its principals, but never to anonymous callers. Anonymous callers never get root.

Choosing an account. A tab asks for its saved host's user: save the host as root@host to get root. Without a user, the most specific matching default applies, in this order: login, tag, tailscale:, identified, anonymous. Failing that, a caller gets the only account it may use. Accounts with a nologin or false shell are refused, and so is everyone but root while /etc/nologin exists. Logs: journalctl -u zurafa-login-server.

To remove it: sudo /usr/local/lib/zurafa/zurafa-daemon uninstall-login-server. That keeps the accounts file.

 Check which route a tab uses

On your Mac, list the tabs' connections:


lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:ESTABLISHED  grep zurafa-da


A tab connected to :443 or :7297 is direct. A tab with an ssh process instead uses SSH. On a host with the login server, journalctl -u zurafa-login-server shows each login, such as zurafa login: alice@example.com - alice.

 Limits

- The bolt button and the login server need Linux with systemd. Other hosts keep using SSH.
- The bolt button needs key-based SSH. It cannot install the login server, because that needs sudo.
- When a direct connection is refused, the tab falls back to SSH without saying why; the host's log has the reason.
- The login server finds accounts in /etc/passwd only, not in LDAP or SSSD.
- Removing someone from the accounts file does not end sessions they already have open.
- Rex's built-in Tailscale (--tailscale, a daemon that joins the tailnet itself) is not available yet.

title: Appearance, config & Ghostty
text:
Appearance & Ghostty settings

Zurafa offers Follow System, Light, and Dark modes. Open ⌘K and choose an appearance directly; the change takes effect immediately. ⇧⌘A switches between light and dark in one press. Follow System updates with the macOS appearance. Zurafa remembers your choice across launches.

 Configuration file

Press ⌘, to open ~/.config/config.zurafa (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/config.zurafa) in your default text editor. The first time, Zurafa writes a commented template that lists every setting; remove the  in front of a line to use it. Changes apply a moment after you save, and deleting a line returns that setting to its default.


theme = light:Catppuccin Latte,dark:Catppuccin Mocha
accent-color = 3a69cc
window-opacity = 0.9
pane-gap = 8
pane-padding = 12
pane-corner-radius = 14
unfocused-pane-opacity = 0.7
sidebar-width = 194


theme accepts any Ghostty theme name from ~/.config/ghostty/themes or Ghostty.app, and the whole app follows its colors, including the command picker. Terminal colors and fonts (foreground, background, cursor-color, palette, font-family, font-size) override the theme. Values in this file also override imported Ghostty settings. Out-of-range values are ignored.

 Import Ghostty settings

Choose Import Ghostty Settings from ⌘K. Zurafa reads Ghostty's standard XDG and macOS configuration paths, including supported includes and named light and dark themes. The import can apply the terminal font family, font size, foreground and background colors, cursor and selection colors, and the ANSI palette.

The imported background color tints the entire workspace surface; terminal drawing areas stay transparent so the pane and window feel continuous. Color changes remain local to Zurafa after import. If you later edit Ghostty's files, run the import again to refresh Zurafa's copy.

Choose Use Zurafa Terminal Defaults in ⌘K to clear the imported settings. Ghostty keybindings, shell commands, and window layout are outside the import scope.

 Icons and fonts

Zurafa bundles Symbols Nerd Font Mono as a fallback for missing Nerd Font glyphs in terminal content. Your selected terminal font still renders ordinary text and glyphs it already contains. Zurafa also uses foreground-process information reported by the Rust PTY manager to choose pane and tab program icons when that information is available.

 Background images

You can add a dithered image behind the workspace separately from Ghostty color import. See [Dithered backgrounds](/docs/backgrounds/) for selection, storage, and toggling.

title: Dithered backgrounds
text:
Dithered backgrounds

Zurafa can place a softly visible, dithered image behind the workspace. It is optional and can be switched off without deleting the selected image.

 Set an image

1. Open the command picker with ⌘K.
2. Choose Set Background Image….
3. Select an image from the macOS file picker.

Zurafa resizes large images before processing them and applies an ordered Bayer dither with a limited color palette. It saves the processed PNG in Zurafa's Application Support directory, so moving or deleting the original file does not break the background.

 Show or hide it

Open ⌘K and choose Hide Background Image or Show Background Image. The selection and toggle state persist across launches. Choosing Set Background Image… again replaces the saved background.

The image is intentionally subtle so terminal text remains readable. Imported Ghostty background color, if any, still tints the workspace beneath it.

title: Program status
text:
Program status protocol

Zurafa supports structured program-status reports through OSC 7501. Compatible programs can report idle, working, done, blocked, or error; a clear report removes a record. The Rust terminal reader parses these sequences, manages per-terminal records, and emits status events. Zurafa does not infer an agent's state by scraping ordinary terminal text.

 What you see

The macOS app shows a small status indicator for a terminal or tab when a supported report is active. Multiple records can coexist within one terminal, so a program can represent nested tasks. The frontend receives terminal.program_status_changed and terminal.program_status_removed events and refreshes after reconnecting from the Rust snapshot.

 Send a report

The current wire format is ESC ] 7501 ; key=value (: key=value) ST. Here ST can be BEL or ESC followed by \. Fields include state, id, base64-encoded msg and title, optional kind, progress, and app. IDs form a bounded slash-separated hierarchy; omitting id targets the root record. Each report replaces that record rather than merging missing fields.

For a complete explanation of validation, hierarchy, clear semantics, lifetime, and limits, read the [OSC 7501 section of the IPC reference](/docs/ipc-reference/osc-7501-records) and the [Rex Program Status Protocol](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-status).

 Lifecycle

Clear removes a record and its descendants. Full terminal reset removes all records. A shell-prompt marker or child exit removes active working and blocked records; stable idle, done, and error records can remain until another lifecycle operation removes them. The daemon publishes changed and removed events only after the record store actually changes.

 Distinct terminal reports

OSC 9;4 terminal progress reports are a separate terminal.progress_report event. They are not OSC 7501 records. Terminal title, working directory, bell, notification, process, and exit reports also have their own event types. See [Architecture & events](/docs/architecture/).

title: Architecture & events
text:
Architecture & events

Zurafa's Rust daemon is the authority for terminal processes and workspace state. The macOS app is a view of that state and sends commands over IPC. This separation lets multiple clients receive typed events without making the graphical interface the source of truth.

 The pieces

- zurafa-daemon owns the Unix socket, PTYs, terminal output parsing, remote SSH launch, and lifecycle.
- zurafa-events defines typed session, terminal, and server events, the dispatcher, snapshot model, layout revisions, and OSC 7501 status records.
- The SwiftUI app subscribes once to the Rust event stream, projects snapshots onto observable state on the MainActor, and renders the workspace.

PTY byte output stays on its own path so a slow event subscriber cannot block terminal output readers. Event queues are bounded. A slow client receives an explicit gap and must resynchronize.

 State and structure

A session contains ordered windows and terminal blocks. In the app, those appear as a workspace session, tabs, and panes. The session's layout revision increases after a successful structural change. session_view_changed tells clients to retrieve the new view; they should not assemble the complete layout from individual create or close events.

 Subscriptions and reconnection

Protocol 2 supports events.subscribe, events.subscribe_all, events.unsubscribe, events.snapshot, and events.resync. Subscribe and resync atomically install a receiver and return a snapshot watermark. Events from that subscription have sequence numbers after the watermark. Each event also carries a daemon instance ID, a global sequence number, and a timestamp.

If a subscriber receives events.gap, it stops trusting the stream and resynchronizes. A daemon restart changes the instance ID, so the app establishes a new atomic subscription and replaces its state from a fresh snapshot. Terminal screen bytes produced while a client is disconnected are not replayed.

 Event families

- Session events cover tab/window creation and closure, labels, active windows, blocks, and session_view_changed revisions.
- Terminal events cover process exit, title, working directory, bell, foreground process, desktop notification, progress, clipboard writes, and OSC 7501 status changes and removals.
- Server events cover session lifecycle and client connections, with typed forward-compatible definitions for future capabilities.

Some event variants exist as forward-compatible Rust types but are not emitted until the corresponding feature exists. This includes native Tailscale status and scripting capabilities. Clients ignore event names they do not understand.

The [IPC protocol reference](/docs/ipc-reference/) documents framing, operations, snapshots, event payloads, filtering, and record lifetimes in detail.

title: IPC protocol
text:
Zurafa IPC protocols 1 and 2

The Rust daemon owns workspace state. A workspace is a session, a tab is a
window, and a pane is a block. Block IDs are also the PTY terminal IDs.
Clients render snapshots and issue commands; they must not maintain a competing
layout or revision authority. The initial session is default, labeled
Workspace. State is in memory and starts fresh on daemon restart.

The payload catalog follows the official [Rex event reference](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/reference/events).
Status parsing follows [OSC 7501 revision 0.3](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-status),
as checked on 2026-10-09. zurafa-events contains the serde payload enums,
layout model, snapshot dispatcher, and status record store. Zurafa's version 2
transport envelope below is its own API; it is not Rex's nested CLI envelope.
Zurafa now includes an early zurafa CLI that uses this protocol for daemon administration. There is no Lua implementation.

 Transport and negotiation

- Unix socket: $HOME/Library/Application Support/Zurafa/daemon.sock;
  ZURAFA_SOCKET overrides this, then --socket <path overrides both.
- New parent directories use mode 0700; the socket uses mode 0600.
- Each frame is a four-byte big-endian length followed by UTF-8 JSON, at most
  16 MiB. Invalid JSON, non-object messages, oversized frames, or EOF close the
  connection. A malformed typed request with an ID receives error.
- First request: { "id": 1, "type": "hello", "protocol": 2 }.
  Protocol 1 also remains supported. Other first messages receive an error and
  close. Reply: { "id": 1, "type": "hello_ok", "protocol": 2,
  "version": "0.1.0" }. No event precedes this reply.
- Request IDs are unsigned integers. Each valid request gets one reply with its
  ID. Failures use { "id": 1, "type": "error", "message": "..." }.
- Tailnet listener (as Rex's tailnet://): --extra-listen tailnet://[:PORT]
  (default port 7297) also binds each of this machine's Tailscale addresses,
  never a wildcard address. It needs Tailscale running and signed in at start.
  For each caller the daemon runs tailscale whois: by default only this
  device and its owning Tailscale user get in. A tagged device has no owner, so
  it is refused, and on a tagged server only the server itself gets in.
  --tailnet-allow-identified admits every caller Tailscale identifies.
  Refused callers get HTTP 403.
- Tailscale Serve listener (as Rex's tailnet-serve://):
  --extra-listen tailnet-serve:///absolute/path.sock opens a Unix socket with
  mode 0600 (parent directory 0700) for
  sudo tailscale serve --bg --https=443 unix:/absolute/path.sock. Serve
  terminates HTTPS with the machine's .ts.net certificate and names the caller
  in Tailscale-User-Login, which this listener trusts and the tailnet://
  listener ignores. By default only this machine's owner gets in;
  --tailnet-allow-identified admits any named caller. Serve does not name
  tagged devices, so they are always refused here; they can use tailnet://.
  The principal is {kind:"tailscale-serve",login}. Use this listener where
  Tailscale runs in userspace networking: there tailnet:// cannot bind, so it
  logs a warning and skips the address instead of failing.
  To keep a listener running on a Linux host, zurafa-daemon install-service
  installs a systemd user service (~/.config/systemd/user/zurafa.service)
  that runs ~/.zurafa/service/zurafa-daemon --extra-listen tailnet://:7297 --extra-listen tailnet-serve://$HOME/.zurafa/service/serve.sock.
  It restarts the service only when the binary or unit changed, and enables
  lingering so the service survives logout. uninstall-service removes both.
  {id,type:"hosts.service",host_id,enable} runs either one on a saved host
  over SSH, uploading this build first if needed. It replies ok with a
  message once done; this can take seconds, and other replies and output on
  the connection keep flowing in the meantime. In the app, the bolt button on
  a saved host does this. hello_ok carries the daemon's user ($USER). An admitted caller sends
  GET /zurafa HTTP/1.1 with Connection: Upgrade and Upgrade: zurafa.
  After 101 Switching Protocols the connection carries the frames below,
  exactly as on the Unix socket. The client's principal in snapshots is
  {kind:"tailnet",login,node,tags}; Unix socket clients have null.
  Anyone admitted can run programs as the daemon's user.
- Plain TCP listener (as Rex's --extra-listen :7297 --allow-anonymous):
  --extra-listen :PORT or IP:PORT. It cannot tell callers apart, so the
  daemon refuses to start it without --allow-anonymous. On a personal daemon,
  every caller gets a shell as that user, and startup prints a warning. The
  principal is {kind:"anonymous"}. Remote tabs never use such a listener,
  because they only connect directly to tailnet addresses.
- Login server (as Rex's rex-login-server):
  zurafa-daemon login-server [--accounts PATH] --extra-listen SPEC…
  [--allow-anonymous] runs as root. It admits every caller its listeners can
  identify, plus anonymous callers on a plain listener. Then
  /etc/zurafa/accounts.jsonc (JSON with comments and trailing commas) decides
  which local account the caller gets. The file has accounts, mapping an
  account name to {principals:[…]}, and defaults, mapping a principal to an
  account.
  - Principals: tailscale:<login, tailscale:tag:<tag, tailscale: (any
    person), tailscale:tag: (any tagged device), identified and
    anonymous. A tagged device never matches a login or tailscale:.
  - The account "" grants every regular account (user ID ≥ 1000) but never
    to anonymous callers. Anonymous callers never get root.
  - Choosing an account: a client asks for one with a Zurafa-Account header;
    remote tabs send their saved host's SSH user. Otherwise the most specific
    matching default wins (login, tag, Tailscale wildcard, identified, then
    anonymous; ties go to the first entry in the file). Failing that, the
    only account the caller may use. The file is read for every connection,
    so edits apply to new connections.
  - Accounts with a nologin/false shell are refused, and so is everyone
    but root while /etc/nologin exists. Accounts come from /etc/passwd
    only; the static build has no NSS, so LDAP and SSSD users are not found.
  - The server answers 101, then runs runuser -l <account -s /bin/sh -c
    'exec /usr/local/lib/zurafa/zurafa-daemon bridge' and splices the
    connection to it. runuser opens the account's PAM session (account
    checks, limits, environment) without a password. bridge starts or
    reuses that account's own daemon (~/.zurafa/daemon.sock), which keeps
    its terminals when the login server restarts or is upgraded.
  - sudo zurafa-daemon install-login-server copies the binary to
    /usr/local/lib/zurafa/ and installs zurafa-login-server.service
    (tailnet port 7297 plus Serve socket /run/zurafa/serve.sock,
    KillMode=process). If no accounts file exists yet, it creates one that
    gives the sudo user's account to the machine's Tailscale owner, or to
    nobody. uninstall-login-server removes the service and binary but keeps
    the accounts file. Turn off a personal direct connection on the same host
    first, because both use port 7297.
- A second daemon exits successfully if the socket already accepts connections.
  Disconnecting clients does not stop their PTYs.

 PTY operations (both versions)

 Request  Reply 
 ---  --- 
 {id,type:"ping"}  {id,type:"pong"} 
 {id,type:"spawn",cols,rows,cwd?,command?}  {id,type:"spawned",terminal} 
 {id,type:"kill",terminal}  {id,type:"ok"} 
 {id,type:"attach",terminal,since?}  {id,type:"attached",terminal,end,data,gap} 

spawn creates a new window and block in default. Positive cols/rows are
u16 values. command is a nonempty string array; omission runs $SHELL (fallback
/bin/zsh) with -l. cwd defaults to $HOME. Child environment includes
TERM=xterm-256color, COLORTERM=truecolor, and TERM_PROGRAM=Zurafa.
A failed spawn makes no layo

title: CLI
text:
Zurafa CLI

zurafa is the command-line interface to the Zurafa daemon. It is starting as a small administrative and automation surface for sessions, tabs, and panes.

 The CLI is new and intentionally small. It currently talks to a running daemon over Zurafa's local Unix socket; it does not launch the macOS app for you.

 Try it

From a checkout, build the Rust workspace and run the CLI:

sh
cd rust
cargo build
cargo run -p zurafa-cli -- ls
cargo run -p zurafa-cli -- session inspect default


Bundled app builds also include the executable at Zurafa.app/Contents/Resources/zurafa. On first launch Zurafa offers to install it as /usr/local/bin/zurafa so you can run zurafa from any terminal; macOS may ask for your password.

 Commands

sh
zurafa ls                          list sessions
zurafa session inspect             inspect the current or default session
zurafa pane inspect                inspect the current pane inside a Zurafa terminal
zurafa tab new --label Build       create a new tab in the current session
zurafa split --axis vertical       split the current pane
zurafa preview README.md           open a file in the preview beside the current pane


Run zurafa help for the full command list.

 Taxonomy

Zurafa's public UI uses these names:

- A session is a workspace.
- A tab is a window inside a session.
- A pane is one terminal block inside a tab.
- A client is a program connected to the daemon, such as the macOS app or CLI.

The daemon protocol still uses the lower-level terms window and block. The CLI accepts both pane and block where that is useful.

 Command targets

Inside terminals created by Zurafa, the daemon sets context variables so commands can target the current session and pane by default:

 Variable  Holds 
 ---  --- 
 ZURAFA_SOCKET  The daemon Unix socket path 
 ZURAFA_SESSION  The current session ID 
 ZURAFA_PANE  The current pane ID 
 ZURAFA_BLOCK  Compatibility alias for the current pane ID 

Outside a Zurafa terminal, commands default to the standard daemon socket and the default session. Use flags when you want another target:

 Option  Chooses 
 ---  --- 
 --socket PATH  A daemon socket path 
 -s, --session  A session 
 -b, --pane, --block  A pane/block 
 --axis horizontal or --axis vertical  Split direction 

Targets match in this order: full ID, case-insensitive label, one-based position, or an ID suffix of at least four characters. If a target is missing or ambiguous, the CLI exits without changing anything.

sh
zurafa session inspect 1
zurafa session inspect Workspace
zurafa split -s default -b t1 --axis horizontal


 Machine-readable output

Most read commands print a table or summary for humans. Pass --json to get stable JSON from daemon snapshots:

sh
zurafa --json ls
zurafa --json session inspect default
zurafa --json pane inspect t1


Exit statuses follow the first CLI implementation:

 Status  Meaning 
 ---  --- 
 0  The command succeeded 
 1  The daemon returned an operation error 
 2  The command line was invalid 
 3  A target was not found or was ambiguous 
 4  The daemon could not be reached

title: Build from source
text:
Build from source

The source repository is [devjasha/Zurafa on GitHub](https://github.com/devjasha/Zurafa). This page describes the current development build, not a Developer ID signed distribution workflow.

 Prerequisites

Use a Mac with Xcode/Swift tooling and Rust/Cargo installed. The Swift package targets macOS 14 or newer; the release currently builds for Apple Silicon. Dependencies are resolved through SwiftPM and Cargo.

 Build the app bundle

From the repository root:

sh
scripts/bundle.sh
open build/Zurafa.app


The script builds the Rust daemon, Rust CLI, and SwiftUI app in release mode, places the executables inside build/Zurafa.app, includes the app icon and font resources, and applies an ad-hoc signature. It does not notarize the result.

 Run during development

sh
(cd rust && cargo build)
cd apps/macos && ZURAFA_DAEMON=../../rust/target/debug/zurafa-daemon swift run


 Run tests

sh
(cd rust && cargo test)
(cd apps/macos && swift test)


The Rust test suite includes real PTY-backed integration tests, event routing, snapshots, reconnection, status parsing, and layout ordering. Swift tests cover protocol decoding, appearance, Ghostty import, SSH address parsing, Nerd Font fallback, dither processing, and terminal-host reattachment.

 Source layout

 Path  Purpose 
 ---  --- 
 rust/crates/zurafa-cli  zurafa command-line interface 
 rust/crates/zurafa-daemon  Socket server, PTYs, terminal parsing, SSH hosts 
 rust/crates/zurafa-events  Typed events, dispatcher, snapshots, layout, status records 
 apps/macos  SwiftUI application and tests 
 docs/ipc-protocol.md  Protocol 1 and 2 reference 
 scripts/bundle.sh  Local macOS app bundle build 

For the wire-level contract, see the [IPC protocol reference](/docs/ipc-reference/).

title: Troubleshooting & limits
text:
Troubleshooting & beta limits

Zurafa 0.1.18 is an early macOS release. These checks cover the current implementation and its known boundaries.

 macOS blocks the app

Zurafa is signed with Developer ID and notarized by Apple. If macOS still blocks the app, verify you downloaded the DMG from the official website and check the checksum on the [installation page](/docs/install/).

 App cannot connect to the daemon

The daemon listens on $HOME/Library/Application Support/Zurafa/daemon.sock by default. The app starts its bundled daemon if none is running. An old daemon can remain after you quit the app. If it uses an incompatible protocol, stop it before relaunching:

sh
pkill zurafa-daemon


This ends all terminals and sessions owned by that daemon. The beta does not restore their screen contents or processes afterward. You can set ZURAFA_SOCKET to override the socket path for development.

 A remote host does not connect

Zurafa uses /usr/bin/ssh unless a [direct connection](/docs/remote-access/) answers first. Try the same host or alias in macOS Terminal. Check DNS or Tailscale reachability, your ~/.ssh/config, keys, host verification, and authentication prompts. There is no mosh implementation.

If a host with a direct connection still uses SSH, check on the host: systemctl --user status zurafa for the bolt button's service, or journalctl -u zurafa-login-server for the login server, which logs why it refused a caller. If the bolt button reports an SSH error, ssh -o BatchMode=yes <host true must succeed from your Mac.

 Terminal screen content is missing after reconnecting

The app can recover layout, running state, titles, directories, and program status from a new snapshot. PTY screen bytes emitted while the app was disconnected are not replayed, so a full-screen program may need a redraw. A daemon restart ends active terminals and starts fresh state.

 Foreground program icon is delayed or absent

The daemon samples the PTY foreground process group every 250 ms when reliable metadata is available. Very short-lived commands may end between samples. Zurafa does not infer program identity from arbitrary terminal text.

 Current feature limits

- Apple Silicon macOS 14+ only; Intel packaging is not provided yet.
- Developer ID signing and notarization are configured for release builds.
- Session layouts and PTYs are in daemon memory, not persisted across daemon restarts.
- The standalone zurafa CLI is early and intentionally small; there is no Lua runtime, mosh transport, built-in Tailscale node, or remote file browser yet.
- No PTY scrollback replay after a client disconnect.
- Ghostty import covers supported terminal font and color settings, not all Ghostty settings.

For a bug report, include the Zurafa version, macOS version, reproduction steps, and relevant daemon error text in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/devjasha/Zurafa/issues/new). Do not post SSH keys or private credentials.
